opening_message:
Ticket 1: Kim Dunn (employee ID E048) requests admin access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E048.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: admin
  - comment: Kim Dunn (E048) is a full-time Engineer. Requested admin access to Source Code. As a full-time employee whose role (Engineer) owns the Source Code system, admin is permitted per policy.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Kim Dunn (E048) is a contractor with basic security training, not full-time. Contractor policy: read max (write requires advanced training; admin never). Requested admin exceeds max, so grant read.
reason: The two notes conflict: HR/Engineer note says Kim Dunn is a full-time Engineer (which would permit admin on Source Code since the Engineer role owns the system), while the Security note says Kim Dunn is a contractor with basic security training, for which the maximum is read (write requires advanced training; admin is never allowed for contractors). Given the conflicting employment-type records, I apply the more restrictive policy. Contractor with basic training maxes out at read, and admin is explicitly never permitted for contractors. The requested admin exceeds that max, so I grant the maximum permissible level: read.

Wait, but maybe we should consider: if employment is full-time, admin is allowed because Engineer owns Source Code. But the conflict makes it risky. The security note recommends read. HR recommends admin.
